{{Short description|Geometry theorem relating to triangles}}
[[File:Hinge theorem.svg|400px|right]]
In [[geometry]], the '''hinge theorem''' (sometimes called the '''open mouth theorem''') states that if two sides of one [[triangle]] are [[congruence (geometry)|congruent]] to two sides of another triangle, and the [[Congruence (geometry)#Congruence of triangles|included angle]] of the first is larger than the included angle of the second, then the third side of the first triangle is longer than the third side of the second triangle.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Moise|first1=Edwin|last2=Downs, Jr.|first2=Floyd|title=Geometry|date=1991|publisher=Addison-Wesley Publishing Company|isbn=0201253356|page=[https://archive.org/details/geometry00mois/page/233 233]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/geometry00mois/page/233}}</ref> This theorem is given as Proposition 24 in Book I of [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's ''Elements'']].

== Proof from the law of cosines ==

The theorem is an immediate corollary of the [[law of cosines]].<ref name=ahh>{{cite journal |journal=Journal of Geometry |title=The open mouth theorem, or the scissors lemma, for orthocentric tetrahedra |year=2012 |volume=103 |pages=1–16 |last1=Abu-Saymeh |first1=Sadi |last2=Hajja |first2=Mowaffaq |last3=Hayajneh |first3=Mostafa |doi=10.1007/s00022-012-0116-4 }}</ref>  For two triangles with sides <math>\{a, b, c\}</math> and <math>\{a, b, \hat c\}</math> with angles <math>\gamma</math> and <math>\hat \gamma</math> opposite the respective sides <math>c</math> and <math>\hat c</math>, the law of cosines states:

<math display=block>\begin{align}
c^2 &= a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos \gamma, \\
\hat{c}^2 &= a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos \hat \gamma.
\end{align}</math>

The [[cosine]] function is [[monotonically decreasing]] for angles between <math>0</math> and <math>\pi</math> [[radian]]s, so <math>\hat\gamma > \gamma</math> implies <math>\hat c > c</math> (and the converse as well).

== Scope and generalizations ==

The hinge theorem holds in [[Euclidean space]]s and more generally in simply connected non-positively curved [[space form]]s.

It can be also extended from plane Euclidean geometry to higher dimension Euclidean spaces (e.g., to [[tetrahedra]] and more generally to [[simplices]]), as has been done for [[Orthocentric tetrahedron|orthocentric tetrahedra]] (i.e., tetrahedra in which altitudes are concurrent){{r|ahh}} and more generally for orthocentric simplices (i.e., simplices in which altitudes are concurrent).<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hajja|first=Mowaffaq|author2=Mostafa Hayajneh|title=The open mouth theorem in higher dimensions|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|date=August 1, 2012|volume=437|issue=3|pages=1057–1069|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2012.03.012|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Converse ==

The [[Conversion (logic)|converse]] of the hinge theorem is also true: If the two sides of one triangle are congruent to two sides of another triangle, and the third side of the first triangle is greater than the third side of the second triangle, then the included angle of the first triangle is larger than the included angle of the second triangle.

In some textbooks, the theorem and its converse are written as the [[solution of triangles|SAS]] Inequality Theorem and the [[solution of triangles|SSS]] Inequality Theorem respectively.
